title: Turn-of-month equity timing - SPY during the month-end/month-start flow window, IEF otherwise
card_json: {"asset_classes":["us_etf"],"author_agent":"scout","data_requirements":[{"dataset":"sharadar_sfp","fields":["ret_co","ret_oc","tradable"],"frequency":"1d","period":["2002-08-01","2020-12-31"]}],"falsification_criteria":["Net Sharpe on dev (primary k=2, m=3) below the 60/40 SPY/IEF Sharpe + 0.10, or the one-sided 90 % bootstrap CI of the Sharpe difference includes 0.","At costs x2 the primary configuration no longer beats the 60/40 Sharpe.","Fewer than 75 % of the neighbor configurations (days_before 1/3, days_after 2/4 and their combinations) beat the 60/40 Sharpe.","Fewer than 2 of 3 dev sub-periods beat the 60/40 Sharpe, or one block holds more than 60 % of the log return.","Mechanism: the strategy does not beat the 95th percentile of random-entry runs with the same exposure and turnover, i.e. holding SPY on 5 random trading days per month earns as much as holding it in the turn-of-month window.","Mechanism: on dev, the mean daily SPY return inside the window minus the mean daily SPY return outside the window is not positive; or the post-2008 (after McConnell-Xu) Sharpe excess over 60/40 is less than half the pre-2008 excess."],"family":"turn-of-month-flows","holding_period":{"rebalance":"monthly","typical_days":10},"market_exposure":"long_only","mechanism":{"counterparty":"Liquidity-driven sellers (mutual funds, pension plans, institutions meeting month-end cash needs) who sell at temporarily depressed prices before the turn, and the market makers/intermediaries who absorb that flow and are paid for it; plus investors holding equities through the rest of the month who bear full equity risk for little premium. The sellers keep doing it because their payment dates and mandates are fixed: they cannot postpone payouts, and holding large cash buffers all month costs them more than the price impact.","why":"The monthly payment cycle creates predictable, market-wide price pressure. Institutions that must deliver cash for month-end payments (pension and benefit payouts, fund redemptions, distributions) sell liquid equities and bonds in the days before month end, when settlement still guarantees cash by the last day; prices are pushed down and revert as the payment date passes. Right after the turn, payroll-driven retirement contributions and reinvested coupons/dividends arrive and are invested in equities in the first days of the new month. Both effects concentrate the equity premium in a short window around the turn of the month (last trading days of month M plus first trading days of M+1); outside the window the equity premium is small, so holding intermediate Treasuries there gives a better risk/return trade-off than holding equities all month. This is a long-only timing of the equity sleeve of a stock/bond portfolio by a calendar that is known in advance, not a forecast.","why_not_arbitraged":"The pressure is market-wide, so it cannot be hedged cross-sectionally: harvesting it means carrying full directional equity risk for a premium of roughly a tenth of a percent per day, which ties up risk capital of intermediaries with balance-sheet limits. Most investors are mandate-bound to stay invested (benchmark-relative funds) or rebalance far less often than twice a month. The anomaly is old and well-known, so the risk is decay, which the publication-decay and holdout checks test."},"notes":"Gap named in prior_studies: calendar and flow effects were never tested by the owner; nothing in the registry. Differences from killed studies: no trend, momentum, inverse vol or regime filter (studies 2, 9, 10); no stock selection (1, 5, 11); the timing input is the exchange calendar only, so there are no estimated signals to overfit and no look-ahead path. Primary window k=2, m=3 is chosen a priori between the classic Lakonishok-Smidt/McConnell-Xu window (-1..+3) and the Etula et al. account in which the month-end selling pressure peaks a few days before the last trading day and reverts afterwards; the grid brackets both. Expected SPY share ~5/21 = 24 % of days, IEF the rest; total exposure 100 %. Cost risk: ~24 full switches per year (one-way turnover ~48x/y) is only plausible because SPY and IEF are the cheapest tier; costs x2 is the most likely gate to fail. References: the first three predate dev; McConnell-Xu (2008) is inside dev and is the meaningful publication-decay split. Etula et al. was published in 2020 (working paper circulated years earlier), so its post-publication slice of dev is under a year and uninformative. Suggested alternative universe for G2: IVV for SPY and TLT or AGG for IEF (same mechanism, different instruments). Most likely death: the window premium has decayed since the effect became widely known and IEF-outside-window does not compensate, so the Sharpe excess over 60/40 is below +0.10, or it hinges on one sub-period.","references":[{"cite":"Ariel (1987) A monthly effect in stock returns, Journal of Financial Economics","year":1987},{"cite":"Lakonishok, Smidt (1988) Are seasonal anomalies real? A ninety-year perspective, Review of Financial Studies","year":1988},{"cite":"Ogden (1990) Turn-of-month evaluations of liquid profits and stock returns: a common explanation for the monthly and January effects, Journal of Finance","year":1990},{"cite":"McConnell, Xu (2008) Equity returns at the turn of the month, Financial Analysts Journal","year":2008},{"cite":"Etula, Rinne, Suominen, Vaittinen (2020) Dash for cash: monthly market impact of institutional liquidity needs, Review of Financial Studies","year":2020}],"signal":{"description":"Instruments: SPY (equity sleeve) and IEF (bond sleeve). Calendar: XNYS trading days; the calendar (including holidays) is known in advance, so the window membership of every day is known before it starts and no price data is used to decide anything. For every calendar month M, label the trading days around the turn: the last trading day of M is day -1, the second-to-last is day -2, ...; the first trading day of M+1 is day +1, the second is day +2, .... The turn-of-month window of M is the set of trading days {-k, ..., -1, +1, ..., +m} (k = days_before, m = days_after), i.e. k + m consecutive trading days. Target weights: on every trading day inside a window hold 100 % SPY and 0 % IEF; on every other trading day hold 0 % SPY and 100 % IEF. Execution: the target of trading day d is decided after the close of the previous trading day d-1 and traded at the open of d. Concretely, sell IEF and buy SPY at the open of day -k (decision after the close of day -k-1); hold SPY through the close of day +m; sell SPY and buy IEF at the open of day +m+1 (decision after the close of day +m). The P&L of the switch day therefore uses ret_oc of the instrument bought and ret_co of the instrument sold. Two switches per month, about 24 per year, both legs fully switched (no partial weights, no volatility scaling, no other filter). Start: the first full month after both SPY and IEF have prices (IEF starts in mid 2002); before that the strategy holds nothing and is not evaluated. Missing data: if either instrument has no tradable price on a scheduled switch day, keep the current position and switch at the next open where both are tradable; if the window has already ended by then, skip that window. No other instruments are ever traded.","params":{"days_after":{"grid":[2,3,4],"value":3},"days_before":{"grid":[1,2,3],"value":2}}},"title":"Turn-of-month equity timing - SPY during the month-end/month-start flow window, IEF otherwise","universe":{"instruments":["SPY","IEF"],"kind":"instruments"}}

title: Front-running month-end 60/40 rebalancing - SPY vs IEF spread in the last days of the month, direction set by month-to-date drift
card_json: {"asset_classes":["us_etf"],"author_agent":"scout","data_requirements":[{"dataset":"sharadar_sfp","fields":["ret_co","ret_oc","tradable"],"frequency":"1d","period":["2002-08-01","2020-12-31"]}],"falsification_criteria":["Net Sharpe on dev (primary window_days 5) below 0.5, or the one-sided 90 % bootstrap CI of the Sharpe difference vs T-bill includes 0.","Fewer than 75 % of the neighbor configurations (window_days 4 and 6) reach net Sharpe 0.5 vs T-bill, or their median Sharpe is below 0.7 x the primary.","Net Sharpe at costs x2 below 0.5.","Mechanism, equity leg - the SPY leg alone (SPY weight times SPY return over the window, IEF leg removed) has a non-positive mean return on dev; the paper locates the pressure mainly in equities, so if only the bond leg earns, the rebalancing story is wrong.","Mechanism, placebo window - the same rule applied to a mid-month window (decision after trading day 5 of the month using month-to-date drift, holding trading days 6-10) earns a net Sharpe of at least 0.7 x the month-end Sharpe; then the effect is generic short-term reversal of the stock/bond spread, not month-end rebalancing flow.","More than 60 % of the dev log return comes from one of the three sub-period blocks (e.g. a single crisis year carrying the result)."],"family":"rebalancing-flow-pressure","holding_period":{"rebalance":"monthly","typical_days":5},"market_exposure":"long_short","mechanism":{"counterparty":"Calendar rebalancers (defined-benefit pensions, balanced and target-date mutual funds, multi-asset mandates) whose policy documents fix both the target weights and the rebalancing schedule. They pay the price impact knowingly or unknowingly because tracking their policy portfolio, governance and benefit cash needs matter more to them than a few basis points of execution cost per month.","why":"Pension funds, balanced funds, target-date funds and other fixed-weight stock/bond mandates rebalance on a calendar schedule, much of it in the last week of the month (benefit payments and month-end valuation). The direction and size of their trade is mechanically determined by the month-to-date drift of stocks versus bonds: after stocks outperformed bonds they must sell equities and buy bonds, after stocks underperformed they must buy equities and sell bonds. These are large, price-insensitive orders concentrated in a few days, so they create temporary price pressure on the equity/bond spread (Harvey, Mazzoleni, Melone document roughly -17 bp next-day equity return per one-standard-deviation calendar rebalancing signal on S&P 500 and 10y Treasury futures). The strategy takes the other side in advance: it holds the spread the rebalancers will push, and closes at the month-end close when their flow is done.","why_not_arbitraged":"The flow is enormous (trillions in fixed-weight mandates) relative to the risk capital willing to pre-position against it for a few days; the per-month edge is small compared with the spread's volatility, so a front-runner bears real risk for a modest Sharpe. Rebalancers cannot easily change behaviour: schedules are written into investment policy statements and are slow to change, and switching to threshold or smoothed rebalancing has its own costs and committee overhead."},"notes":"Gap from prior_studies: calendar and flow effects. Relation to H-0001 (turn-of-month-flows, rejected at G1): H-0001 was an unconditional long-equity bet on month-end/month-start cash inflows. This card is a different mechanism: an asset-allocation rebalancing flow whose sign is set by month-to-date relative performance, traded as a dollar-neutral spread that is short equities about as often as long, and it is flat during the first days of the month (the turn-of-month inflow window). If the Chair nevertheless counts it in turn-of-month-flows, that is acceptable. Not short-term reversal as in studies 5-7: the signal is a month-to-date (about 15 trading days) cross-asset drift, timed to the month-end calendar, and the placebo-window criterion tests exactly that distinction. Costs: two very liquid ETFs, about 24 round trips of gross 1.0 per year. Exposure: gross 1.0 for about 5 of 21 trading days, mean gross exposure about 0.24 (above the 0.20 minimum for the primary; window_days 3 and 4 are below it and are only robustness neighbors). Position entries about 2 per month x about 220 months. Sample starts after IEF's first price (2002-07-30). The reference is a 2025 working paper, outside dev, so no publication-decay split is possible in dev; the holdout (2021-2026) is mostly pre-publication. Suggested alternative universe for G2: IVV/TLT or VTI/IEF (same mechanism, different instruments).","references":[{"cite":"Harvey, Mazzoleni, Melone (2025) The Unintended Consequences of Rebalancing, NBER Working Paper 33554","year":2025}],"signal":{"description":"Instruments: SPY (equity leg) and IEF (bond leg), daily total returns from sharadar_sfp. Calendar: XNYS trading days. For each calendar month m let L be the last trading day of m and K = window_days. The window is the last K trading days of month m (L-K+1 .. L). Decision day t = the trading day immediately before the window (the (K+1)-th last trading day of m). After the close of t, compute the month-to-date total returns of SPY and IEF from the close of the last trading day of month m-1 to the close of t (compounded daily total returns), and D = R_SPY_mtd - R_IEF_mtd. If D > 0 (stocks outperformed, rebalancers will sell stocks / buy bonds): weights SPY -0.5, IEF +0.5. If D < 0: SPY +0.5, IEF -0.5. If D == 0 or either instrument has a missing return on any day from the start of month m to t, or either instrument is not tradable on the entry day: stay flat for that month. Entry at the open of the first window day (t+1). Exit: the whole position is closed at the close of L (a pre-scheduled calendar trade that uses no data; the month-end close is when calendar rebalancers execute). If the backtester cannot execute at the close, the only permitted fallback is to exit at the open of the first trading day of month m+1. Outside the window the strategy is flat (cash, earning the T-bill rate if the framework credits cash). Weights are fixed during the window (no daily rebalancing within the window). Gross exposure is 1.0 in the window and 0 outside, dollar-neutral. One decision per month; no other parameters, thresholds or filters.","params":{"window_days":{"grid":[3,4,5,6,7],"value":5}}},"title":"Front-running month-end 60/40 rebalancing - SPY vs IEF spread in the last days of the month, direction set by month-to-date drift","universe":{"instruments":["SPY","IEF"],"kind":"instruments"}}

title: Volatility-timed equity exposure - SPY when short-term SPY volatility is below its long-run level, IEF otherwise, weekly
card_json: {"asset_classes":["us_etf"],"author_agent":"scout","data_requirements":[{"dataset":"sharadar_sfp","description":"SPY daily total returns; history before IEF exists is used only to fill the volatility windows.","fields":["ret_co","ret_oc"],"frequency":"1d","instruments":["SPY"],"period":["1999-01-04","2020-12-31"]},{"dataset":"sharadar_sfp","description":"IEF daily total returns, the defensive asset in the stressed state.","fields":["ret_co","ret_oc"],"frequency":"1d","instruments":["IEF"],"period":["2002-07-30","2020-12-31"]}],"falsification_criteria":["Net Sharpe on dev below the 60/40 SPY/IEF Sharpe + 0.10, or the one-sided 90 % bootstrap CI of the Sharpe difference includes 0.","Fewer than 75 % of the neighbor configurations (short window 10 or 42, long window 126 or 504, and their combinations) beat the 60/40 Sharpe.","Fewer than 2 of 3 dev sub-period blocks beat 60/40, or one block contributes more than 60 % of the log return.","Sharpe at costs x2 below the 60/40 Sharpe, or below the 95th percentile of random-entry runs with the same switching frequency and SPY exposure.","Mechanism: SPY's annualized mean daily return divided by its variance (reward per unit of variance) over the days spent in the calm state is not higher than over the days spent in the stressed state; then volatility does not forecast lower risk-adjusted equity returns and the rule is not volatility timing.","Mechanism: with IEF replaced by zero return (cash) in the stressed state, the strategy's Sharpe is not above SPY buy-and-hold Sharpe; then the result is driven by Treasury flight-to-quality returns, not by avoiding equity variance."],"family":"volatility-managed-exposure","holding_period":{"rebalance":"weekly","typical_days":40},"market_exposure":"long_only","mechanism":{"counterparty":"Investors whose risk-bearing capacity is reduced exactly when volatility spikes (levered and margin-constrained investors, funds hit by redemptions, VaR- and drawdown-limited desks) sell equities into high-volatility periods without being compensated proportionally; and static-weight investors who keep the same equity share regardless of the risk they are carrying, thereby holding the most variance when its compensation is lowest. The premium is slow to adjust because expected-return beliefs move more slowly than realized volatility.","why":"Equity volatility is highly persistent at horizons of weeks, but the equity premium does not rise in proportion to it: when short-term realized volatility jumps above its long-run level, expected returns per unit of risk (mean/variance) are low, and when volatility is calm they are high (Moreira and Muir 2017; Fleming, Kirby and Ostdiek 2001). A rule that holds equities only while short-term volatility is not elevated, and Treasuries otherwise, therefore earns most of the equity premium with a lower share of equity variance, which raises the risk-adjusted return relative to a static 60/40 mix that keeps a constant equity weight through volatility spikes.","why_not_arbitraged":"Exploiting it means increasing equity exposure in calm markets and cutting it after volatility spikes, which large balanced mandates and benchmarked managers cannot do (tracking-error limits against a static policy portfolio), and which looks pro-cyclical and loses during sharp V-shaped rebounds that occur while volatility is still high. The edge is a modest Sharpe improvement, not an arbitrage, and it carries the risk of whipsaw around volatility regime changes."},"notes":"Gap named in prior_studies.md (\"volatility-managed exposure\" not tried). Different from the killed trend filters (study 2: 9-ETF inverse-vol allocation with per-class trend filters, whose loss vs 60/40 came from holding many low-Sharpe risk assets; study 9: crypto SMA filter): the signal here uses no price level or past return, only the ratio of short- to long-run realized volatility, and the risky asset is SPY alone. The threshold is the natural one (short-run vol equal to its own long-run level, computed point-in-time), not tuned. Binary switching rather than continuous 1/variance scaling is chosen so that the strategy has discrete position entries (expected several regime switches per year, i.e. well over 100 entries and over 36 trading decision dates), and no leverage is needed. Cederburg et al. (2020) is cited as the main counter-evidence: volatility management does not improve Sharpe out of sample for many factors, although the market factor is among the better cases; the literature prior (+20 trials) is accepted. Known risk: in the dev period stock-bond correlation is mostly negative, so IEF tends to rally in the stressed state; the second mechanism criterion is there to separate that from the volatility-timing effect. Costs: SPY and IEF are among the most liquid ETFs, a few switches per year.","references":[{"cite":"Moreira, Muir (2017) Volatility-Managed Portfolios, Journal of Finance","year":2017},{"cite":"Fleming, Kirby, Ostdiek (2001) The Economic Value of Volatility Timing, Journal of Finance","year":2001},{"cite":"Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang, Yan (2020) On the performance of volatility-managed portfolios, Journal of Financial Economics","year":2020}],"signal":{"description":"Inputs: daily total returns of SPY and IEF from sharadar_sfp. Daily close-to-close total return of day d is r_d = (1 + ret_co_d) * (1 + ret_oc_d) - 1, where ret_co_d is previous close to open of d and ret_oc_d is open to close of d. Decision dates: the last trading day of each calendar week (XNYS calendar), after its close t, using only data up to and including that close. On each decision date compute sigma_short = sample standard deviation of SPY daily log total returns over the last short_window_days trading days ending at t, and sigma_long = the same over the last long_window_days trading days ending at t (days without a SPY bar, e.g. vendor-error days dropped by the loader, are simply skipped; the window then extends back to collect the required number of valid returns). Rule: if sigma_short <= sigma_long the target portfolio is 100 % SPY, 0 % IEF (\"calm\" state); otherwise 100 % IEF, 0 % SPY (\"stressed\" state). There is no other threshold, no leverage and no cash leg; gross exposure is always 1. Trades are executed at the open of the next trading day t+1; positions are held until the next decision date that changes the state (no trade when the state is unchanged). Start: SPY history from the beginning of its data period is used only to fill the volatility windows; the strategy is evaluated from the first decision date on which IEF has a price and both windows are full. If either instrument has no tradable bar at the open of t+1, the previous holdings are kept and the switch is executed at the next open on which both are tradable.","params":{"long_window_days":{"grid":[126,252,504],"value":252},"short_window_days":{"grid":[10,21,42],"value":21}}},"title":"Volatility-timed equity exposure - SPY when short-term SPY volatility is below its long-run level, IEF otherwise, weekly","universe":{"instruments":["SPY","IEF"],"kind":"instruments"}}

title: Crypto new-listing supply overhang - short recently listed Binance pairs, long seasoned pairs, dollar-neutral, weekly

They keep doing it because each listing is a new story and outcomes are highly skewed (a few listings do rise a lot).","why":"Tokens reach a large exchange when attention and optimism about them peak, while their tradable float is still small and most of the supply (team, investors, treasury, ecosystem allocations) is locked and vests over the following months. Right after listing the coin cannot be shorted (no margin borrow, perp contracts arrive later or with thin open interest), so the price is set by the most optimistic buyers (Miller 1977 disagreement + short-sale constraints). As short constraints relax and vested supply is sold, the price drifts down relative to seasoned coins. This is the crypto analogue of long-run IPO underperformance (Ritter 1991) and of post-lockup selling, and the long-run underperformance of the median listed ICO token has been documented directly (Momtaz). The strategy is long an equal-weight basket of seasoned coins and short an equal-weight basket of coins listed 2 weeks to 3 months ago, so the generic altcoin beta largely cancels and what remains is the listing-age spread.","why_not_arbitraged":"Shorting new listings is hard and expensive exactly in the window where the overpricing is largest (no borrow, then high borrow/funding costs, squeeze risk from the small float); the short leg has unbounded upside risk and fat right tails, which deters capital-constrained arbitrageurs; capacity is small because new listings are thin; and early holders sell for liquidity/vesting reasons regardless of price."},"notes":"Why this is not a re-run of prior studies: studies 9 and 10 sorted crypto on past returns (trend, momentum) and their short legs were time-series trend shorts; this card sorts only on listing age, never on returns, and the long leg is seasoned altcoins (not BTC), so the altcoin beta is mostly hedged. Known data caveats, all biased against the hypothesis: (1) the listing date is the first USDT-pair bar, so coins that traded on Binance against BTC earlier and only got a USDT pair later are wrongly counted as new listings, which dilutes the short leg; (2) delisted pairs are only partly in the archive, so the worst recent listings (those delisted soon after a collapse) are partly missing from the short leg; (3) the -2 % delisting convention credits a short only 2 %. Implementation caveat for the Skeptic: shorting spot pairs is a modelling simplification; live execution would use USD-M perpetuals (binance_perp_1d and binance_funding have no loader yet), and borrow/funding costs on the short leg are not in the cost model. skip_days exists for the same reason: the first days after listing are typically not shortable and are dominated by listing-day volatility. Most likely ways to die: short squeezes in an altcoin bull phase concentrate the loss in one sub-period, or the dev window (crypto dev ends 2022-12-31) is too short for G3 with the 20-trial literature prior. No dates, episodes or specific coins were used to design it.","references":[{"cite":"Momtaz, P. P. (2021) The pricing and performance of cryptocurrency. European Journal of Finance 27(4-5)","year":2021},{"cite":"Ritter, J. R. (1991) The long-run performance of initial public offerings. Journal of Finance","year":1991},{"cite":"Miller, E. M. (1977) Risk, uncertainty, and divergence of opinion. Journal of Finance","year":1977}],"signal":{"description":"Data: binance_spot_1d, daily bars closing at 00:00 UTC. Listing date of a pair = the first UTC day on which it has a bar in the dataset (point-in-time: known from that day on). Listing age on day t = calendar days between the listing date and t. Decision schedule: weekly, after the close of each Sunday UTC bar (the bar ending Monday 00:00 UTC), using only data up to and including that bar; trades are executed at the open of the next bar (Monday) and held until the next weekly decision. Eligible set on decision day t: the pairs in the loader's crypto_top_n(100) universe as of t (ranking by trailing quote volume known at t; if the loader does not rank point-in-time, rank by median daily quote_volume over the 30 days ending at t), that have a bar on t. Short leg S: eligible pairs with skip_days <= listing age <= max_age_days. Long leg L: eligible pairs with listing age >= 365 days (fixed constant, \"seasoned\"). Missing data: a pair without a bar on the execution day keeps its previous weight until it trades again; a pair handled as delisted by the loader (gap > 7 days) is closed at the loader's delisting price and is not re-entered. title: Stablecoin net issuance as crypto inflow gauge - hold liquid Binance coins only while aggregate USD stablecoin supply is growing, weekly

Fallback / cross-check: sum of the current supply metric (SplyCur) of USDT and USDC from the free Coin Metrics community API. Needed from the earliest available date (2017 or 2018) to today; signal series only, not tradable. Clock: crypto (value for UTC day d known at 00:00 UTC of d+1); the strategy lags it by one further day. Forward source: the same free API, updated daily, so G5 paper trading is possible.","fields":["total_circulating_usd"],"frequency":"1d","period":["2018-01-01","2022-12-31"]}],"falsification_criteria":["Net Sharpe on dev below BTC buy-and-hold Sharpe + 0.10, or the one-sided 90 % bootstrap CI of the Sharpe difference includes 0.","Neighbor lookbacks (14 and 56 days) do not beat BTC buy-and-hold (fewer than 75 % of neighbors).","Fails at costs x2 or below the 95th percentile of random entries with the same exposure and turnover.","More than 60 % of the log return comes from one of the three dev sub-periods.","Mechanism: the stablecoin signal adds nothing beyond price trend - the same strategy with the regime set by the sign of the BTC trailing 28-day log return instead of G_t has an equal or higher net Sharpe on dev; then the result is the already-killed crypto trend filter (prior study 9) in disguise.","Mechanism: risk-off weeks (G_t <= 0) do not have a lower mean forward 1-week return of the risk-on portfolio than risk-on weeks."],"family":"stablecoin-flow-pressure","holding_period":{"rebalance":"weekly","typical_days":7},"market_exposure":"long_only","mechanism":{"counterparty":"Holders who stay fully invested while net capital is leaving the system (they bear the drawdowns of outflow phases, often retail buy-and-hold and illiquid-alt holders), and late buyers who enter after prices have already absorbed an inflow. In outflow phases the strategy sells to dip buyers who rely on price alone.","why":"USD stablecoins are the main funding currency of crypto spot markets: fiat that enters the crypto trading system is first minted into a stablecoin and then spent on coins over the following days and weeks, and capital that leaves is redeemed (supply is burned). Net issuance is therefore a direct, public measure of aggregate net capital flow into the asset class, unlike price trend, which only measures its effect. Crypto markets are thin relative to these flows and have no fundamental anchor, so demand is inelastic and flows move prices (inelastic-markets argument of Gabaix and Koijen applied to a market with no valuation arbitrageurs). Minted balances are deployed gradually (OTC desks, exchange deposits, staged buying), so the price pressure follows issuance with a lag; when supply shrinks, capital is leaving and the remaining holders absorb the selling. The strategy holds coins while the trailing net issuance is positive and sits in cash while it is negative.","why_not_arbitraged":"Shorting most coins is costly or impossible on spot, perpetual funding is volatile, and crypto has no large valuation-based arbitrage capital with a mandate to lean against flows. The signal is public but noisy at daily frequency (treasury mints in large round batches, chain migrations), so it is only usable as a slow multi-week regime filter, which has low capacity value for fast arbitrageurs and is uncomfortable for funds benchmarked to BTC because it can sit in cash during rallies."},"notes":"Why the new dataset is essential: the mechanism is about capital flows into the crypto system, and the only daily, public, point-in-time measure of those flows is stablecoin net issuance; no field in the catalog (prices, volumes, funding) measures fund flows, and using price trend instead would be prior study 9 (crypto trend filter, killed). Difference to study 9: that signal was BTC's own price relative to its moving average; this one is an exogenous flow quantity that can diverge from price (supply grows while prices fall when new money buys a dip, shrinks during rallies driven by leverage). The mechanism falsification criterion explicitly compares against the price-trend version so the test dies for an informative reason if the flow signal is just trend. Lineage: Griffin and Shams link Tether issuance to subsequent BTC price increases (a manipulation interpretation for the early period); this card uses aggregate issuance of all USD stablecoins as an organic flow gauge, and the publication-decay check (2020 inside dev) applies. Universe of 10 pairs with inverse-volatility weights and a 0.25 cap keeps the portfolio near BTC/ETH risk, satisfies the sentinel weight limit, and yields >100 position entries from regime switches and weekly membership changes. Weekly rebalancing of top-10 liquid pairs keeps costs moderate. Threshold 0 and lookback 28 days are round, untuned choices. Risk acknowledged: dev covers only 2018-2022 for this signal (about 260 weekly decisions), so the bootstrap CI may be wide.","references":[{"cite":"Griffin, Shams (2020) Is Bitcoin Really Untethered? Journal of Finance","year":2020},{"cite":"Gabaix, Koijen (2021) In Search of the Origins of Financial Fluctuations: The Inelastic Markets Hypothesis","year":2021}],"signal":{"description":"Inputs: (a) S_d = total circulating supply in USD of all USD-pegged stablecoins at the end of UTC day d (new dataset stablecoin_supply_1d); (b) Binance spot daily bars (close, quote_volume, ret_oc, ret_co). Schedule: weekly decisions after the daily close of every Sunday UTC day t (the bar ending 00:00 UTC Monday); trades at the open of day t+1 (Monday bar open); positions held until the next weekly decision. Point-in-time: the strategy uses the supply value of day t-1 (one extra day of lag against late snapshots), i.e. G_t = ln(S_{t-1} / S_{t-1-L}) with L = lookback_days calendar days. If S is missing on t-1, use the last available value at or before t-1; if fewer than L+1 days of supply history exist, or the last available value is older than 7 days, the strategy is in cash. Regime: risk-on if G_t > 0, risk-off otherwise (fixed threshold 0, not tuned). Universe at each decision: the top 10 Binance USDT spot pairs (stablecoins and wrapped assets excluded by the loader) by median daily quote_volume over the 30 UTC days ending at t, among pairs with at least 60 daily bars up to t. Pairs not yet listed are not eligible; a pair that stops trading is exited at the loader's delisting rule. Weights when risk-on: inverse volatility, w_i proportional to 1 / sigma_i with sigma_i the standard deviation of daily close-to-close log returns over the 60 days ending at t; weights normalised to sum to 1, then capped at 0.25 per pair with the excess redistributed proportionally to uncapped pairs (repeat until no weight exceeds 0.25). Gross exposure = 1, long only. Weights when risk-off: all weights 0 (cash). Rebalancing: at every weekly decision the target weights are recomputed and traded in full.","params":{"lookback_days":{"grid":[14,28,56],"value":28}}},"title":"Stablecoin net issuance as crypto inflow gauge - hold liquid Binance coins only while aggregate USD stablecoin supply is growing, weekly","universe":{"kind":"crypto_top_n","n":10}}

title: Crypto liquidation-flush rebound - buy liquid coins after an extreme daily drop, only while BTC is in a weekly uptrend, hold 3 days
card_json: {"asset_classes":["crypto_spot"],"author_agent":"scout","data_requirements":[{"dataset":"binance_spot_1d","description":"Tradable universe, the BTCUSDT weekly regime, the daily trigger and P&L.","fields":["close","ret_co","ret_oc","quote_volume"],"frequency":"1d"},{"dataset":"binance_perp_1d","description":"Mechanism diagnostic only, not used by the trading rule: daily funding of the perp matching each triggered spot pair (<PAIR>.P), where the perp exists (from 2019-12).","fields":["funding"],"frequency":"1d"},{"dataset":"binance_1h_features","description":"Mechanism diagnostic only, not used by the trading rule: UTC session log returns of the trigger day, to tell concentrated (cascade-like) drops from diffuse ones; then the leverage-bias condition carries no information and the regime filter is just a trend filter (already killed in study 9).","Mechanism (deleveraging): among triggers with a matching perp, those where the perp's funding on day t is below its mean of days t-7..t-1 (leverage being flushed) do not have a higher mean forward return than those where it is not.","Mechanism (cascade shape): among triggers covered by binance_1h_features, drops where the worst UTC session carries at least two thirds of the day's log decline (jump-like) do not rebound more than diffuse drops."],"family":"short-term-reversal","holding_period":{"rebalance":"daily","typical_days":3},"market_exposure":"long_only","mechanism":{"counterparty":"Over-leveraged long perp traders (mostly retail, high leverage) whose positions are closed at market by the liquidation engine at the worst price, plus stop-loss and panic sellers in spot who demand immediacy at the bottom of the cascade. They keep doing it because high leverage in a rising market is profitable most of the time and liquidation is involuntary once margin is gone.","why":"In crypto, a large share of open interest is leveraged perpetual-futures positions with exchange-enforced margin. When the market is in an uptrend, leverage is overwhelmingly long (traders chase the trend and pay funding to hold it), so an extreme down day is disproportionately a liquidation cascade: the exchange liquidation engine sells at market regardless of price, each forced sale pushes price into the next liquidation level, and arbitrageurs transmit the perp selling to spot. This is price pressure from forced, information-free sellers (the crypto analogue of the fire sales in Coval and Stafford 2007, and of the liquidity spirals in Brunnermeier and Pedersen 2009). Price pressure of this kind is temporary: once the leverage is flushed the selling stops and prices partly revert over the next days, and whoever supplies liquidity in the flush is paid for it (Nagel 2012: returns to liquidity provision rise when liquidity evaporates). The weekly regime filter is part of the mechanism, not a tuning device: in a downtrend leverage is more balanced or short, and large drops are more often information or de-risking that continues (consistent with the time-series momentum documented for crypto), so those drops are not bought.","why_not_arbitraged":"Supplying liquidity into a cascade means catching a falling knife: the drop may continue (a real crash, a hack, an exchange failure), so the trade has large left-tail risk exactly when market makers' and funds' risk budgets are hit and when their own leverage is being cut (Brunnermeier and Pedersen). Capital that can act within a day across many altcoins is limited, the edge is per-event and volatile, and many crypto funds have mandates or drawdown limits that prevent buying after large losses."},"notes":"Brief: crypto, 1-5 day holding, combined timeframes. The weekly BTC regime gates a daily extreme-move entry (timeframes 1w + 1d); hourly-derived session returns are used only as a pre-registered mechanism diagnostic, to avoid a fourth tuned threshold in the rule. Family: filed under short-term-reversal on purpose. The economic mechanism (being paid for supplying liquidity to price-insensitive sellers) is the same as in the owner's studies 5-7 (stock reversal, reversal when VIX > 25), so their trials should count against it. What is different and why it is worth a run: (a) the sellers are identifiable and truly forced (margin liquidations on 24/7 leveraged perps), not generic order imbalance; (b) study 7 concluded that the VIX-conditioned effect was the market bounce, not stock selection; this card does not try cross-sectional selection, it is a long-only timing of the bounce itself and is judged against BTC buy & hold and random entries with the same exposure and turnover; (c) the regime filter conditions on the side of leverage, which is a crypto-specific reason for the bounce, not a tuned trend filter. Known counter-evidence: Liu and Tsyvinski (Risks and returns of cryptocurrency, RFS) find time-series momentum in crypto at weekly horizons, so unconditional dip-buying should lose; the card bets that extreme one-day moves in long-leveraged regimes are dominated by forced flow. If it dies, the diagnostics say whether the regime, the deleveraging fingerprint or the cascade shape carried any information. Main risks: costs (about one entry per day of 0.25 weight in regime ON, 3-day holds: annual turnover is high and costs x2 is a hard gate); mean exposure near the 20 % floor because the strategy is in cash whenever the regime is OFF and no pair has triggered; few pairs exist in 2017-2018, so early dev contributes few trades. Perpetuals were considered and rejected for the long leg: in uptrend regimes funding paid by longs is high and would be a direct cost of exactly these trades; spot carries no funding.","references":[{"cite":"Coval, Stafford (2007) Asset fire sales (and purchases) in equity markets, Journal of Financial Economics","year":2007},{"cite":"Brunnermeier, Pedersen (2009) Market liquidity and funding liquidity, Review of Financial Studies","year":2009},{"cite":"Nagel (2012) Evaporating liquidity, Review of Financial Studies","year":2012}],"signal":{"description":"Data: binance_spot_1d daily bars (UTC days, close at 00:00 UTC). Decisions after the close of day t using data up to that close; trades at the open of day t+1. (1) Universe on day t: the 50 USDT spot pairs with the highest mean daily quote_volume over the 30 days ending at t, among pairs with at least 60 days of price history at t (stablecoins and wrapped assets already excluded by the loader). If fewer than 50 pairs qualify, use all that qualify. (2) Weekly regime (1w): weeks run Monday 00:00 UTC to Sunday 24:00 UTC; the weekly close is the BTCUSDT daily close of the Sunday. At each weekly close compute SMA_N = mean of the last regime_weeks weekly closes of BTCUSDT (including the current one). Regime is ON for the whole following week if the weekly close is strictly above SMA_N, OFF otherwise (OFF until regime_weeks weekly closes exist). The regime used on day t is the one set at the last weekly close on or before t. (3) Daily trigger (1d): for each pair i in the universe, r_i,t = log(close_t / close_t-1) and sigma_i,t = the standard deviation of daily log returns over the 30 days ending at t-1 (today excluded). Pair i triggers on day t if regime is ON and r_i,t <= -k_sigma * sigma_i,t. Pairs with a missing close on t or t-1, or fewer than 30 return observations, do not trigger. (4) Positions: a trigger opens a long position at the open of t+1 that is held for hold_days days and closed at the open of t+1+hold_days. A new trigger on a pair already held does not add a second position; it resets the exit date to hold_days days after the new entry. Positions already open are held to their exit date even if the regime turns OFF or the pair leaves the top 50. (5) Weights: every day each open position gets weight 1 / max(4, n_open), where n_open is the number of positions open after today's entries and exits (so at most 0.25 per pair and gross <= 1). Weights are recomputed daily; the remainder is cash (earns the T-bill rate per the engine). Long only, no leverage. (6) If a held pair has no bar (delisting or gap), the engine's delisting rule applies.","params":{"hold_days":{"grid":[1,2,3,4,5],"value":3},"k_sigma":{"grid":[1.5,2.0,2.5,3.0],"value":2.0},"regime_weeks":{"grid":[10,20,30,40],"value":20}},"selection_procedure":"None. The primary configuration (k_sigma 2.0, hold_days 3, regime_weeks 20) is pre-registered; the grid only serves the G2 neighbor test. Universe size 50 and the 30-day volatility and volume windows are fixed conventions, not tuned.","timeframes":["1w","1d"]},"title":"Crypto liquidation-flush rebound - buy liquid coins after an extreme daily drop, only while BTC is in a weekly uptrend, hold 3 days","universe":{"kind":"crypto_top_n","n":50}}

title: Intraday-component reversal confirmed by intraday-component momentum - weekly long/short in LIQ-500, buy last week's intraday losers among 12-month intraday winners, short the mirror
card_json: {"asset_classes":["us_equity"],"author_agent":"scout","data_requirements":[{"dataset":"sharadar_sep","description":"LIQ-500 point in time; ret_oc for signals, ret_oc and ret_co for P&L; alt universe sp500 for G2.","fields":["ret_oc","ret_co","tradable","listed","delisting"],"frequency":"1d","period":["1998-01-02","2020-12-31"]}],"falsification_criteria":["Net Sharpe on dev (costs x1) below 0.5, or not above T-bill by the G1 bootstrap bound.","Net Sharpe at costs x2 below 0.5 (the edge does not pay for weekly turnover).","Fewer than 75 % of the grid neighbors (fast_days 3/10, slow_days 126/504 and their combinations) reach Sharpe 0.5 net.","More than 60 % of the dev log return comes from one of the three sub-periods (in particular the 1998-2005 block that dominated study 5).","Mechanism check 1 (decomposition): the identical construction using close-to-close returns for IR_fast and IR_slow has a net Sharpe at least as high as the intraday version; then the intraday split adds nothing and this is study 5 again.","Mechanism check 2 (confirmation): the unconditional intraday reversal (long bottom quintile / short top quintile of IR_fast over the whole eligible set, no slow split) has a net Sharpe at least as high; then the slow timeframe adds nothing.","Mechanism check 3 (overnight placebo): sorting on the overnight component (sum of ln(1+ret_co)) instead of ret_oc in the fast window gives a reversal spread of the same size; then the news/trading distinction is not what drives it."],"family":"short-term-reversal","holding_period":{"rebalance":"weekly","typical_days":5},"market_exposure":"market_neutral","mechanism":{"counterparty":"Liquidity demanders who need immediacy within the week: funds meeting redemptions or inflows, index and risk-model rebalancers, stop-loss and margin-driven sellers, institutions completing split orders. They accept a temporary price concession; the strategy takes the other side, but only where the slow intraday drift says informed demand is on the strategy's side, so it is less often run over by a continuing informed seller.","why":"A stock's daily return has two parts with different origins. The overnight part (close to next open) mostly reflects news released outside trading hours; the intraday part (open to close) mostly reflects the price impact of investors' own trading. Barardehi, Bogousslavsky and Muravyev show that portfolios formed on past intraday returns display both short-term reversal and medium-term momentum, while portfolios formed on past overnight returns show neither at those horizons. Reading: a sharp intraday move over the last week is mostly temporary price pressure from liquidity-demanding trades (it reverts as liquidity providers are paid), while a persistent intraday drift over the past year is the slow incorporation of informed order flow that others underreact to (it continues). The strategy uses both timeframes of the same trading-driven component: it buys stocks whose last-week intraday return was among the worst while their 12-month intraday return is in the top half (a temporary liquidity push against a persistent informed-demand drift), and shorts the mirror image. Close-to-close reversal (lab study 5) mixes the news part, which does not revert, into the signal; removing it should raise the edge per unit of turnover, which is what decides survival after costs at a weekly horizon.","why_not_arbitraged":"Liquidity provision at a weekly horizon needs balance sheet and bears inventory risk exactly when liquidity is scarce (reversal profits are highest in stressed markets, when providers withdraw). Turnover of roughly 50x per year caps the capacity and keeps large asset managers out; the residual premium is the compensation for that risk and for costs, which is why it is small in large caps and must be measured net of costs x2."},"notes":"Brief fit: short holding (5 trading days), US single stocks, cross-sectional, two timeframes (a 1-week fast reversal signal confirmed by a 12-month slow momentum signal, both computed from daily bars). Relation to prior work: study 5 (short-term reversal with a trend filter) died on DSR (N = 993), on validation and on profit concentration in 1999-2002. This card is honestly in the same family (short-term-reversal) and accepts that trial count. The mechanism-level difference is the return decomposition: both the reversal and the confirming trend are computed only from the trading-driven intraday component, because the news-driven overnight component is not expected to revert at a one-week horizon and only dilutes the signal (more turnover per unit of edge). The slow filter is not a price trend of the market or of the stock's total return but the stock's own 12-month intraday drift (informed-flow proxy), applied symmetrically to both legs. Mechanism checks 2 and 3 are written so that a death says which half of the story failed. Known risks, stated up front: (a) profits of reversal strategies are reported to accrue largely overnight (Lou, Polk and Skouras on the tug of war between overnight and intraday returns); trading at the open of t+1 misses the first night after the signal, which may be the strongest; (b) pre-decimalization cost multiplier x2.5 hits the 1998-2001 part, so the strategy cannot live off that era; (c) short legs of high-intraday-return losers are crash-prone in sharp junk rallies. No hindsight: no dates or names are used, the universe is the PIT LIQ-500, parameters are round conventional values. No new data needed.","references":[{"cite":"Lehmann, B. N. (1990) Fads, Martingales, and Market Efficiency, Quarterly Journal of Economics","year":1990},{"cite":"Barardehi, Y. H., Bogousslavsky, V., Muravyev, D. What Drives Momentum and Reversal? Evidence from Day and Night Signals (SSRN working paper)","year":2022},{"cite":"Nagel, S. (2012) Evaporating Liquidity, Review of Financial Studies","year":2012}],"signal":{"description":"Data: sharadar_sep daily ret_oc (open-to-close return of day d), ret_co (close of d-1 to open of d, only for P&L), tradable, listed, PIT liquidity rank. Universe: point-in-time liq_n with n = 500. Decision dates: the last trading day of each calendar week (XNYS), after the close of that day t, using data up to and including the close of t; orders are executed at the open of t+1 and held to the open after the next decision date (about 5 trading days). Inputs per stock i (log intraday returns l_d = ln(1 + ret_oc_d), missing days count as 0): IR_fast_i = sum of l_d over the last fast_days trading days d = t-fast_days+1 .. t. IR_slow_i = sum of l_d over trading days d = t-slow_days+1 .. t-21 (the most recent 21 trading days are skipped so the slow window does not overlap the reversal window). Eligibility at t: member of the PIT LIQ-500 at t, tradable at t, at least 90 % of the days of the slow window and of the fast window with a valid ret_oc (stocks listed for less than slow_days are not eligible). Construction (double sort): split the eligible set at the cross-sectional median of IR_slow into W (top half) and L (bottom half). Long leg: the 20 % of W with the lowest IR_fast. Short leg: the 20 % of L with the highest IR_fast (rounded to the nearest integer, at least 10 names per leg, otherwise flat that week). Weights: +0.5 / n_long on each long, -0.5 / n_short on each short (dollar-neutral, gross 1.0, no leverage). Ties broken by instrument id. Holding: positions are held unchanged until the next decision date; at each decision date the whole book is re-formed and only the differences are traded. A stock not tradable at the open of t+1 is skipped (its weight stays in cash). A delisting during the hold realizes the dataset's terminal return and the weight goes to cash until the next decision date. P&L uses total returns (ret_co and ret_oc compounded); unadjusted prices are not used.","params":{"fast_days":{"grid":[3,5,10],"value":5},"slow_days":{"grid":[126,252,504],"value":252}},"selection_procedure":"None. Primary configuration fixed a priori (one-week reversal window, 12-month momentum window with a 1-month skip, the conventional choices); quintile legs within halves are a fixed convention, not a parameter.","timeframes":["1d","1w","1mo"]},"title":"Intraday-component reversal confirmed by intraday-component momentum - weekly long/short in LIQ-500, buy last week's intraday losers among 12-month intraday winners, short the mirror","universe":{"kind":"liq_n","n":500}}

title: Earnings-announcement premium via volume seasonality - weekly LIQ-500 long/short, long stocks whose volume 52 and 13 weeks ago predicts an announcement next week
card_json: {"asset_classes":["us_equity"],"author_agent":"scout","data_requirements":[{"dataset":"sharadar_sep","description":"Daily dollar volume for the volume-seasonality signal and total returns for P&L. The first ~15 months are warm-up (52 weeks + 21 trading days of history needed before the first prediction).","fields":["ret_co","ret_oc","dollar_volume","tradable","listed","delisting"],"frequency":"1d","period":["1998-01-02","2020-12-31"]}],"falsification_criteria":["Net Sharpe on dev (costs x1) below 0.5 versus T-bill, or the one-sided 90 % bootstrap lower bound of the Sharpe excess is at or below zero.","At costs x2 the net Sharpe falls below the T-bill benchmark bar (the premium per event is smaller than twice the round-trip half-spread).","Fewer than 75 % of the neighbors (av_threshold 1.5 / 3.0, tol_days 1 / 5 and their combinations) beat the benchmark, or their median Sharpe is below 0.7 x the primary.","Mechanism (the predictor) - in the holding weeks, the median over weeks of the long basket's mean max-AVn over the 5 holding days is not at least 1.5 x that of the short leg; then the rule does not identify announcements and the test is uninformative about the premium.","Mechanism (timing placebo) - the same rule with both lags shifted by 6 weeks (annual lag 364+42 days, quarterly lag 91+42 days, i.e. mid-quarter, non-announcement weeks) earns a Sharpe of at least half the primary; then the return does not come from announcement timing but from selecting high-volume stocks.","The strategy does not beat the 95th percentile of 200 random-entry baskets with the same number of names, turnover and exposure.","More than 60 % of the log return comes from one of the three dev sub-periods, or the post-2007 (post-publication) Sharpe is below half the pre-2007 Sharpe."],"family":"earnings-announcement-premium","holding_period":{"rebalance":"weekly","typical_days":5},"market_exposure":"market_neutral","mechanism":{"counterparty":"Attention-driven buyers (retail and momentum-chasing traders) who buy announcers at elevated prices around the event, and holders who keep announcement risk without being paid for it; on the short side, nobody in particular - the short leg is the rest of the liquid universe and hedges market and size exposure.","why":"Stocks earn abnormally high returns in the few days around their scheduled earnings announcements (Frazzini and Lamont 2007; Savor and Wilson 2016; Barber, De George, Lehavy and Trueman 2013). Two non-exclusive explanations: (1) attention-driven buying - the announcement puts the stock in the news, small investors who buy what catches their attention (Barber and Odean 2008) but rarely sell short push prices up around the event, and the premium is largest in stocks whose past announcements drew the most abnormal volume (Frazzini-Lamont); (2) a priced risk - announcers' cash-flow news is informative about the market, so their covariance with the market spikes and investors demand a premium to hold them through the event (Savor-Wilson). Announcement dates are highly persistent: a firm reports in the same week of the same fiscal quarter year after year, and its announcement day is usually the highest-volume day of its quarter. So a stock's own daily dollar volume, read on two slower clocks (the same week one year ago and about one quarter ago), predicts next week's announcers point-in-time without any announcement-date data. The annual lag pins the calendar; the quarterly lag confirms that the past spike was a recurring scheduled event and not one-off news (M&A, guidance shock, index inclusion).","why_not_arbitraged":"The premium is small per event and is paid for bearing event risk: announcer returns have fat-tailed idiosyncratic jumps, so a concentrated weekly book has high idiosyncratic volatility and needs breadth and constant turnover; short-horizon capital (stat-arb desks) tends to cut gross exposure into announcements precisely because of jump risk, and long-only mandates cannot hold the hedged spread. If the Savor-Wilson risk explanation is right, the premium is compensation and should persist."},"notes":"Fit to the brief: holding 5 trading days, US single stocks, cross-sectional in LIQ-500 (ticker-blind, uses only each stock's own volume history), and genuinely multi-timeframe: a daily volume event measured against a quarterly baseline, located on an annual (52-week) calendar and confirmed on a quarterly (13-week) one, traded weekly. Not the short-term-reversal family (study 5, H-0007): the signal uses no past returns at all, only the timing of scheduled information events. Not turn-of-month / calendar timing of the market (H-0001, H-0002): the calendar is stock-specific and the book is dollar-neutral, so it isolates the cross-sectional premium rather than market timing. No new data needed: sharadar_sf1 has filing dates (no loader, and 10-Q filing dates lag the earnings press release by weeks, so they would be the wrong clock anyway); inferring the announcement calendar from volume seasonality is point-in-time by construction. av_threshold carries the Frazzini-Lamont attention channel (higher past announcement volume -> larger premium); 2.0 and the grid are round values, not fitted. Honest cost arithmetic: each event costs about 2 x half-spread (3-6 bps tiers) on the long weight, so the strategy needs a weekly announcer-minus-rest spread of roughly 20-30 bps per event to survive costs x2; the literature premium is of that order in broad samples but is reported to be stronger in smaller stocks than in LIQ-500 names, and pre-decimalization costs (x2.5 until 2001-04) hit the first sub-period. Most likely death: G1/G2 cost stress (premium in large caps smaller than costs x2) or G1 Sharpe below 0.5 because the idiosyncratic jump risk of a 10-40 name announcer basket swamps a small premium. Either way the predictor check and the timing placebo make the death informative.","references":[{"cite":"Frazzini, Lamont (2007) The earnings announcement premium and trading volume, NBER Working Paper 13090","year":2007},{"cite":"Savor, Wilson (2016) Earnings announcements and systematic risk, Journal of Finance","year":2016},{"cite":"Barber, De George, Lehavy, Trueman (2013) The earnings announcement premium around the globe, Journal of Financial Economics","year":2013},{"cite":"Barber, Odean (2008) All that glitters: the effect of attention and news on the buying behavior of individual and institutional investors, Review of Financial Studies","year":2008}],"signal":{"description":"Inputs: daily dollar_volume, ret_co, ret_oc, tradable of sharadar_sep stocks (all history the loader provides for each stock, also before it entered the universe). Decision once a week after the close of the last trading day of the calendar week (normally Friday), using data up to that close; trades at the open of the first trading day of the next week; positions are held until the next weekly rebalance (5 trading days in a normal week). Step 1, daily abnormal volume (1d with a ~1q baseline): for stock i on trading day d, AV(i,d) = dollar_volume(i,d) / median(dollar_volume(i, d-63 .. d-1)) (needs at least 40 valid days in the 63-day window, else undefined). Normalize by the market: AVn(i,d) = AV(i,d) / median over all stocks of the LIQ-500 universe on day d of AV(j,d) (removes market-wide spikes such as option-expiry, index-rebalance and crash days). Step 2, event days: d is an event day of stock i if AVn(i,d) >= av_threshold AND AVn(i,d) is the maximum of AVn(i, .) over trading days d-21 .. d+21 of that stock (the highest-volume day of its ~quarter). Only days with d+21 <= t are ever evaluated, which holds for all lags below (no look-ahead). Step 3, predicted announcers for next week: let D1 .. D5 be the calendar dates Monday .. Friday of the holding week. Stock i is a predicted announcer if (a) annual lag (1y): it had an event day with calendar date in [D1 - 364 - tol_days, D5 - 364 + tol_days] (364 days = 52 weeks, same weekdays), AND (b) quarterly confirmation (1q): it had an event day with calendar date in [D1 - 91 - 10, D5 - 91 + 10] (91 days = 13 weeks; fixed +-10 days because fourth-quarter reports come later than interim reports). Step 4, eligibility: stocks that are LIQ-500 members at the decision close, tradable, and have defined AVn on at least 80 % of trading days in the last 380 calendar days. Stocks failing this are in neither leg. Step 5, weights (dollar-neutral, gross <= 1): long leg = predicted announcers, equal weight w = min(0.05, 0.5 / N_long) each, so long gross L = min(0.5, 0.05 * N_long) (with fewer than 10 names the long leg is scaled down, the rest is cash). Short leg = all other eligible stocks, equal weight, total short gross = L. If N_long = 0 the book is flat that week. Weights are reset to target at each weekly rebalance. Huddart, Lang and Yetman (2009) document elevated volume at the crossing and positive excess returns in the following week (smaller but positive in large caps); George and Hwang (2004) show that nearness to the 52-week high predicts returns, consistent with anchoring-driven under-reaction. Known approximation: investors see the split-adjusted price high, which excludes dividends; the total-return index high differs by at most the dividends of a year and is used so that splits cannot create fake breakthroughs. title: Peer lead-lag catch-up - LIQ-500 market-neutral, long stocks whose return-correlated peers rose last week while they themselves did not move much, short the mirror, hold 5 days

Attention is limited and many investors (and analysts) follow a stock mainly through its own news flow, so a stock whose close peers have repriced, but which has not moved itself, tends to catch up over the following days. In the literature this shows up as industry and connected-firm lead-lag (Hou 2007; Cohen and Frazzini 2008) and as the \"pairs momentum\" component of pairs trading, which Chen, Chen, Chen and Li (2019) show is largely one-month industry momentum and has different dynamics from own-stock short-term reversal. Peers here are found statistically (highest correlation of market-demeaned daily returns), because the lab is ticker-blind and has no industry codes; correlation peers capture industry, supply-chain and style links in one step. The card deliberately removes the own-reversal component (only stocks whose own weekly return is unremarkable can be traded), so what is tested is the diffusion from peers, not reversal again.","why_not_arbitraged":"The signal needs a large peer map and a weekly, fully rotating long/short book of ~120 names; the per-trade edge is small relative to the spread for anyone but low-cost liquidity providers, it is a noisy statistical relation (peers change, correlations are unstable), and it carries industry and style exposure that stat-arb desks usually hedge away, removing exactly this component. Capacity is limited by weekly turnover."},"mechanism_test":{"event":"At a weekly decision date t (last trading day of the calendar week), a stock is in M(t) (eligible, own formation_days return between the 20th and 80th cross-sectional percentile) and its peer return peer[j] (equal-weighted formation return of its peers_k most correlated peers, market-demeaned correlations over corr_window days) is in the top quintile of M(t): side +1; or in the bottom quintile of M(t): side -1. Exactly the entry set of the long and short legs at that rebalance, primary parameters.","horizons":[1,2,5,10,21],"primary_horizon_days":5},"notes":"Brief: short horizon (5 days), US single stocks, cross-sectional, with a mechanism test. Why this is not the short-term-reversal family again (research 5, 7, H-0007, K-0012): the traded names are selected to have an unremarkable own return (middle 60 %), so own reversal is neutralised by construction; the signal is the move of other, correlated stocks, and the predicted sign is continuation of the peers' move (momentum-like), the opposite of reversal. Chen et al. (2019) show the two components have different dynamics. Why not H-0009 (volume-shock news drift): no own news event is needed; the information is in peers' prices. Related lab evidence: the mrel cross-market daily lead-lag scan found nothing out of sample, but it was between liquid index-level markets (ETFs, FX, macro, crypto) where diffusion is fastest; within-stock peer diffusion is a different, attention-based channel and the literature locates it in stocks with less coverage, so the honest risk is that LIQ-500 names are too well covered. Correlation peers are computed only from past returns up to t (point-in-time, ticker-blind, no industry codes needed). Peer map cost: one 500 x 500 correlation per week on <= 504 x 500 floats, cheap. Expected cost: the book rotates most of its names weekly (round trip ~6-12 bps per name at LIQ-500 tiers), which is why the mechanism test's cost ratio is the decisive first check. Three parameters, round values, grid symmetric around the primary. References are cited honestly (adds the literature prior); Hou 2007 is inside dev, so the publication-decay check applies.","references":[{"cite":"Hou (2007) Industry information diffusion and the lead-lag effect in stock returns, Review of Financial Studies","year":2007},{"cite":"Cohen, Frazzini (2008) Economic links and predictable returns, Journal of Finance","year":2008},{"cite":"Chen, Chen, Chen, Li (2019) Empirical investigation of an equity pairs trading strategy, Management Science","year":2019}],"signal":{"description":"Data: daily total return of stock j on day d, r[d,j] = (1 + ret_co[d,j]) * (1 + ret_oc[d,j]) - 1 (ret_co is the overnight return from the close of d-1 to the open of d, ret_oc the open-to-close return of d). Decision dates: the last trading day of each calendar week (t), after the close, using data up to and including the close of t; trades execute at the open of the next trading day t+1; positions are held until the next decision date (about 5 trading days). Eligible set E(t): stocks that are members of LIQ-500 on t, tradable on t, have a non-missing return on each of the last formation_days days, and at least 75 % non-missing daily returns in the last corr_window days. Step 1 (peer map, recomputed at every decision date): over the trailing corr_window trading days ending at t, take r[d,j] for j in E(t), subtract each day's cross-sectional equal-weighted mean over E(t) (market-demeaned returns), and compute the pairwise Pearson correlation on overlapping non-missing days (pairs with fewer than 60 % overlapping days get correlation NaN and are never peers). The peers P(j) of stock j are the peers_k other stocks in E(t) with the highest correlation to j. Step 2 (formation returns): own[j] = compounded return of j over the last formation_days trading days ending at t (days t-formation_days+1 .. t); peer[j] = equal-weighted mean of own[p] over p in P(j). Step 3 (remove own reversal): keep only stocks whose own[j] cross-sectional percentile rank within E(t) is between 0.2 and 0.8 inclusive (the middle 60 %, stocks that did not move much themselves). Weights: long names equal weight +0.5 / n_long, short names equal weight -0.5 / n_short (gross 1, net 0). Names that stay in the same leg keep their target weight (rebalanced to equal weight); names that leave are closed at the open of t+1. A stock that delists while held takes its terminal return and the weight is held in cash until the next decision date. Because short-selling is costly for most of these new investors, more visibility mostly adds buyers, not sellers. Payroll and retirement contributions and reinvested coupons and dividends buy equities at the month turn whatever the price. Institutions that sell before month end to raise cash sell at depressed prices and buy back at the turn (Etula et al. estimate their timing loss in the tens of billions of dollars a year). They do it because their payment schedules are fixed by contracts and mandates, not chosen for returns.","why":"The equity market premium is not spread evenly over the month. Payments in the US are standardized around the turn of the calendar month (wages, pension and 401k contributions, coupons, dividends), so cash that must go into equities arrives in bulk in the last day and first days of each month. In the days just before, institutions sell equities to meet month-end cash needs. Pre-IPO holders sit on large gains, need to return capital to their funds (VC distribution mandates) or to diversify, and sell over the following days; demand for a single stock is downward sloping, so the price gives way. Field and Hanka (2001) found a three-day abnormal return of about -1.5 % and a permanent 40 % rise in volume around the expiry, larger in venture-backed firms. Family: the economic mechanism (locked pre-listing supply becoming sellable after a listing) is the same as H-0004 (crypto new-listing overhang, token unlocks), so this card reuses `new-listing-overhang` instead of opening a new family; it differs from H-0004 by being a dated event with a 5-day hold instead of a listing-age spread, and by trading liquid US stocks with a hedged short. Once the forced trade is done, liquidity providers who took the other side unwind and the price partly reverts. Chen, Noronha and Singal (2004) find the reversal is asymmetric: deleted stocks recover most of their forced-selling loss after the effective date, while additions keep part of their gain. So after the effective date added stocks should lag the cross-section and deleted stocks should beat it. H-0017 (additions only, inside the sp500 universe) had the right sign in every sub-period and a gross effect well above costs, but missed the placebo percentile by a hair with only a few hundred events. This card adds the deletion leg, where the literature puts the larger reversal, to get more events and a second independent source of the same forced-flow mechanism.","why_not_arbitraged":"Pre-effective-date arbitrage (buying additions and shorting deletions after the announcement) is crowded, but supplying liquidity after the event means holding concentrated idiosyncratic single-stock risk for days against a small expected gain, and the capacity is limited by how few events there are. Index changes are lumpy and rare, so no large fund can make this a core strategy."},"mechanism_test":{"event":"A LIQ-500 stock, listed for at least 63 sessions and tradable on t-1 and t, changes S&P 500 membership between t-1 and t (extras alt_universe). Relation to H-0017 and H-0018 (same family, honestly reused, so the trial count accumulates): H-0017 tested additions only in the sp500 universe and missed the placebo bar by a hair (K-0026: sparse events, wide cloud). Its lesson explicitly suggests 'both additions and deletions in one test' for more power. H-0018 tried that inside the sp500 universe and stalled at G0 because a deleted stock is no longer a member (K-0029). This card is the variant H-0018's open question names: the universe is LIQ-500 and S&P membership is only an input (extras alt_universe), so a deleted stock that is still liquid stays inside the declared universe and can be held. Price: additions outside LIQ-500 and deleted stocks that drop out of LIQ-500 are lost; deletions caused by acquisitions mostly vanish because the stock delists. title: Turn-of-month beta rotation, always invested - LIQ-500 long-only, high-beta quintile over the month turn (day -1 to +3), low-beta quintile the rest of the month

The buying pressure concentrates much of the equity premium in a short window around the month turn (Ariel 1987; Lakonishok and Smidt 1988; McConnell and Xu 2008), so market exposure, and therefore beta, is rewarded mainly inside that window. Outside the window the market premium is small, and high-beta stocks are on average overpriced because leverage-constrained and benchmarked investors buy beta through high-beta stocks instead of leverage (Frazzini and Pedersen 2014), so low-beta stocks earn as much or more per unit of risk. A book that holds high-beta stocks only over the month turn and low-beta stocks the rest of the time collects the window premium with leverage-like exposure while avoiding the high-beta discount the rest of the month. The lab's own evidence: the month-turn high-minus-low beta spread cleared the placebo test in H-0016, but a flat-otherwise book could not carry it (K-0027); this card tests it as an always-invested rotation.","why_not_arbitraged":"The window premium is a market-level effect worth a few tenths of a percent per month; capturing it needs timed equity exposure and twice-monthly full rotation, which most mandates (fully invested, low tracking error, low turnover) do not allow. Holding low-beta stocks lags the market in rallies (benchmark risk), the reason the low-beta anomaly persists (Baker, Bradley and Wurgler 2011). Arbitrageurs who would lever the trade face crash risk inside the window (high beta on the wrong days is expensive)."},"mechanism_test":{"event":"A switch decision (after the close of day t): at Switch A (close of the trading day before the month's last trading day) every eligible stock in the top beta leg is an event with side +1 and every stock in the bottom beta leg an event with side -1; at Switch B (close of trading day +post_days of the new month) every stock in the bottom beta leg is an event with side +1 and every stock in the top beta leg an event with side -1. Legs, betas and eligibility exactly as in the signal with the primary parameters. The claim: beta pays inside the window and is penalised just after it.","horizons":[1,2,4,10,15],"primary_horizon_days":4},"notes":"Brief fit: the brief asks for a 1-5 day cross-sectional US stock idea. K-0024 and lessons H-0007..H-0024 say that information and sentiment events in LIQ-500 at 1-5 days are gone (eight dead event studies), and the only short-horizon effect that cleared the placebo bar was the month-turn beta spread (H-0016), which died as a flat-otherwise book because it was invested a fifth of the time (K-0027, K-0030). This card is the follow-up both lessons ask for: the same 4-session window, held as a tilt inside an always-invested book. The window leg is a 4-session hold (inside the brief); the non-window leg has to last the rest of the month (about 17 sessions), so the average hold is about 10 days. That is the closest fit to the brief that has a mechanism the lab has not refuted. Family: turn-of-month-flows (third trial after H-0001 and H-0016), because the new claim is the month-turn flow. The non-window leg is the low-beta stock idea from study 1 (low-volatility family, which failed its holdout). It is here only as the right place to sit when beta is not paid, not as the claim. The mechanism test covers both halves, so if the low-beta leg is wrong just after the window, the test should fail. Requested diagnostics for the Builder and Librarian, if a channel exists: (a) the event study split by Switch A and Switch B events, (b) a static low-beta-quintile book with the same costs as a control, so a pass can be credited to the rotation and not to low beta alone. Parameter values come from the literature (window -1..+3 of Lakonishok-Smidt and McConnell-Xu, 252-day beta, quintiles). They were not tuned, and H-0016's exact primary values are unknown to me. Costs: each switch sells about 100 % and buys about 100 % of the book (2x gross, roughly 10 bps at LIQ-500 half-spreads), 24 switches a year, roughly 2.4 % a year, about 4.8 % at x2. The high-beta leg must earn that back inside the window. Likely ways to die: (1) the window premium faded in the latest third (H-0016), and the low-beta leg lagged the market in the late dev years, so the publication-decay check or the sub-period test fails; (2) costs x2; (3) the high-beta leg on a crash month turn makes the drawdown worse. A ninety-year perspective, Review of Financial Studies","year":1988},{"cite":"Ogden (1990) Turn-of-month evaluations of liquid profits and stock returns: a common explanation for the monthly and January effects, Journal of Finance","year":1990},{"cite":"McConnell, Xu (2008) Equity returns at the turn of the month, Financial Analysts Journal","year":2008},{"cite":"Baker, Bradley, Wurgler (2011) Benchmarks as limits to arbitrage: understanding the low-volatility anomaly, Financial Analysts Journal","year":2011},{"cite":"Frazzini, Pedersen (2014) Betting against beta, Journal of Financial Economics","year":2014}],"signal":{"description":"Universe: point-in-time LIQ-500 members (liq_n, n = 500) on the decision date that are tradable and have at least 189 valid daily returns in the beta window. Beta_i = OLS slope cov(r_i, m) / var(m) over the last beta_lookback trading days ending at the decision close (days where r_i is missing are dropped pairwise). Switch B (out of the window): after the close of day +post_days, rank eligible members by beta and set target weights 1/N on the bottom leg_quantile fraction (lowest beta); trade at the next open (day +post_days+1). that keep the position mechanically, plus buyers who rely on consensus forecasts that are not revised for the delay.","why":"Managers control when they release earnings and tend to delay bad news It used the SF1 10-Q filing, which usually lags the press release by weeks, plus a volume-spike filter as a date proxy, and an accounting earnings change as the surprise. This card uses the real 8-K Item 2.02 reaction session (K-0035) and the market's own reaction as the surprise, so the event is exactly the information release and the test settles whether any post-release drift exists in LIQ-500. It is not H-0009 (volume shocks on any day, gated by holders' capital gain, lost money): events here are only earnings releases, and there is no disposition gate. It is not a reversal card and not a date-prediction card (H-0023, H-0026): no date is predicted, every event is known at the close of its reaction session. Honest prior: K-0039 and Martineau (2022) both point to no drift in large caps after the mid-2000s; the card is filed because the lab's own evidence is a near miss with a bad proxy, and a clean negative here closes the family for liquid stocks. title: Turnover-conditioned short-term momentum - LIQ-500 dollar-neutral, weekly: among the highest-turnover stocks of the past month, long the past-month winners and short the past-month losers, hold 5 days

Predicted next-year release P(r) = the first XNYS session whose calendar date is on or after date(r) + 364 calendar days. The window is the 2*half_window+1 sessions [P - half_window, P + half_window]. (2) Event date. The decision session is t = P - half_window - 1 (the session before the window opens). The stock is eligible only if it is a LIQ-500 member at t, ea_reaction_day has no 1 in the 30 sessions up to and including t (the quarter's release has not already happened early), and all three scores below exist at t. (3) Composite score at t, cross-sectional over all LIQ-500 members at t with all three inputs (no events on a date with fewer than 100 such members): accruals ACC = (netinc - ncfo) / assets; profitability GPA = gp / assets; asset growth AG = assets(t) / assets(t - 252 sessions) - 1 (both values as visible at those dates). Convert each to a percentile rank in [0, 1] among those members; SCORE = (1 - rank(ACC) + rank(GPA) + 1 - rank(AG)) / 3. Side +1 if SCORE is at or above the (1 - leg_quantile) cross-sectional quantile of SCORE on date t, side -1 if at or below the leg_quantile quantile, otherwise no event. The score is frozen at t for the whole window. (4) Positions. A stock with an event is held from the open of P - half_window to the open of P + half_window + 1 (2*half_window+1 sessions), long if side +1, short if side -1, regardless of when the actual release occurs. Each day after the close the book is: long leg = all open long windows, short leg = all open short windows; each leg gets 0.5 gross split equally among its names (dollar-neutral, gross 1). If either leg has fewer than 3 names the whole book is flat that day (no unhedged leg). Weights change only when a name enters or leaves a leg. A stock that delists inside its window takes the engine's terminal return; a stock that leaves LIQ-500 inside its window is closed at the next open. Liquidity providers who absorb that flow demand a price concession, and it is repaid as the forced flow stops and the order book refills, over minutes to hours (Grossman-Miller inventory story; Brunnermeier-Pedersen liquidity spirals). Volatility at the event is high, so modeled slippage is optimistic (catalog known bias); the doubled-cost gate is the guard.
